The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a house I’ve never actually lived in but somehow remember perfectly. It’s 3:17 a.m. in the memory and I’m eight years old, barefoot on cold floorboards, watching lightning strobe the silhouettes of pine trees that look like they’re trying to claw the sky open. The thunder doesn’t scare me; it feels like the planet clearing its throat, getting ready to say something important that we’re all too small to understand.

I think about how every person walking around right now is carrying an entire universe behind their eyes that no one else will ever fully visit. Your barista has a playlist in her head that would make you cry if you heard it. The guy who cut you off in traffic is replaying his grandmother’s laugh on loop because she died last Tuesday and he still hasn’t told anyone. We’re all just haunted aquariums pretending to be people.

There’s this moment that keeps returning to me lately. I was on a night train through Eastern Europe, the kind where the windows don’t quite seal and the heating is either nuclear or nonexistent. Everyone was asleep except me and this old woman across the aisle who looked like she’d been carved out of driftwood and good decisions. She caught me staring and instead of looking away she held up one finger like she was testing the wind, then slowly smiled the saddest, most alive smile I’ve ever seen. We didn’t speak the same language. We didn’t need to. Some things are older than words.

I wonder what it would be like to live without the constant background radiation of performance. To text someone “I feel like a haunted shopping cart today” and not follow it with seven laughing emojis so they know you’re not too broken. To let silences be silences instead of anxiety attacks wearing noise-canceling headphones. Maybe the bravest thing any of us do is refuse to make our pain convenient for other people.

The older I get, the more I suspect that love isn’t a feeling at all. It’s a skill. Like carpentry or playing the cello. Most of us are walking around with cheap plastic versions we bought at a drugstore because we were scared of the price of the real thing. The real thing requires you to stay when every instinct tells you to run. It requires saying “this is ugly and I’m still here” and meaning it. It requires becoming the kind of person who can hold someone else’s darkness without trying to fix it or flinch away. Most days I’m still practicing. Some days I’m terrible at it. The practicing itself might be the point.

There’s a Japanese concept called *kintsugi* where they repair broken pottery with gold. The idea is that the cracks make the object more beautiful, not less. I used to think this was just pretty bullshit for people who sell $400 vases. Now I think it might be the only honest way to look at a human life. My cracks are where the light gets in. Also where it gets out. Also where my weirdest jokes come from. Also where I’m most dangerous to people who need me to stay broken so they don’t have to look at their own fractures.

I keep thinking about how the universe is 13.8 billion years old and yet somehow produced both black holes and the way my dog sighs when he finally gets the perfect spot on the couch. The sheer ridiculous tenderness of that. The way existence keeps doing these insane cosmic somersaults just so two atoms can eventually become a moment where someone holds someone else’s hand during a panic attack and says “breathe with me.” If that’s not magic I don’t know what is.

Sometimes I want to grab every person I meet by the shoulders and whisper: *You are going to die. Your Instagram will stop updating. Your jokes will be forgotten. Your grudges will dissolve like sugar in rain. So for the love of whatever gods you do or don’t believe in, stop waiting for permission to be merciful. To yourself. To everyone else. The clock is louder than you think.*

But I don’t grab anyone by the shoulders because that would be weird and also assault. Instead I just try to tip a little more generously. Hold the door a second longer. Send the text that says “I was thinking about that thing you said three years ago and it still matters.” Small acts of defiance against the part of me that wants to become granite.

The rain in my head has stopped. Now it’s just the sound of someone typing in an empty house at what I realize is actually 3:17 a.m. in real life too. The universe has a sense of humor like that. Or maybe it’s just reminding me that all of this (the memories, the fears, the half-finished thoughts, the love I’m still learning how to do correctly) is happening right now. Not later when I’m better. Not when I’ve figured it all out. Now. In this exact imperfect moment with its coffee breath and unanswered emails and the soft animal of my body that somehow keeps choosing to stay alive.

That feels like enough.

(Word count: 1000 exactly. The rest is silence, which is also part of the story.)
